Before reaching for a specialized algorithm, it pays to look at a graph's basic structure. How big
and how dense is it? How are the degrees distributed? Is it connected, and how far apart are its
nodes? Do hubs link to hubs, or to the periphery? Is there a dense core? These questions have quick
answers, and the answers often decide which analysis comes next. This page covers the methods that
give them.

## The graph at a glance

A graph's printed summary gives its size, density, degree range, and connectivity.
[`describe()`](../reference/Graph.describe.qmd) prints a similar summary, adding whether the graph
is a tree and whether it is bipartite:

```{python}
import edgecase as ec

karate = ec.karate_club()
karate.describe()
```

The same values are available one at a time, for use in code:

| Measure | Method |
|---|---|
| Number of nodes and edges | [`count_nodes()`](../reference/Graph.count_nodes.qmd), [`count_edges()`](../reference/Graph.count_edges.qmd) |
| Density, the fraction of possible edges present | [`density()`](../reference/Graph.density.qmd) |
| Mean degree | [`average_degree()`](../reference/Graph.average_degree.qmd) |
| Degree of every node | [`degrees()`](../reference/Graph.degrees.qmd) |
| Degree of one node | [`get_degree()`](../reference/Graph.get_degree.qmd), [`get_in_degree()`](../reference/Graph.get_in_degree.qmd), [`get_out_degree()`](../reference/Graph.get_out_degree.qmd) |
| Number of nodes of each degree | [`degree_distribution()`](../reference/Graph.degree_distribution.qmd) |
| Nodes with no edges | [`isolates()`](../reference/Graph.isolates.qmd) |

```{python}
karate.count_nodes(), karate.count_edges(), round(karate.density(), 3)
```

The karate club has 78 of the 561 friendships that 34 people could have, a density of about 14%.
Most real networks are much sparser than this: in a network of thousands of nodes, each node is
typically linked to a tiny fraction of the others.

### Properties

A family of `is_*` methods tests a graph for a property and returns `True` or `False`:

| Category | Methods |
|---|---|
| Basic | [`is_directed()`](../reference/Graph.is_directed.qmd), [`is_weighted()`](../reference/Graph.is_weighted.qmd), [`is_simple()`](../reference/Graph.is_simple.qmd) |
| Connectivity | [`is_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_connected.qmd), [`is_strongly_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_strongly_connected.qmd), [`is_weakly_connected()`](../reference/Graph.is_weakly_connected.qmd), [`is_biconnected()`](../reference/Graph.is_biconnected.qmd), [`is_semiconnected()`](../reference/Graph.is_semiconnected.qmd) |
| Trees and acyclicity | [`is_tree()`](../reference/Graph.is_tree.qmd), [`is_forest()`](../reference/Graph.is_forest.qmd), [`is_dag()`](../reference/Graph.is_dag.qmd), [`is_arborescence()`](../reference/Graph.is_arborescence.qmd), [`is_branching()`](../reference/Graph.is_branching.qmd) |
| Regularity | [`is_regular()`](../reference/Graph.is_regular.qmd), [`is_k_regular()`](../reference/Graph.is_k_regular.qmd) |
| Graph classes | [`is_bipartite()`](../reference/Graph.is_bipartite.qmd), [`is_planar()`](../reference/Graph.is_planar.qmd), [`is_chordal()`](../reference/Graph.is_chordal.qmd), [`is_perfect_graph()`](../reference/Graph.is_perfect_graph.qmd), [`is_cograph()`](../reference/Graph.is_cograph.qmd), [`is_split_graph()`](../reference/Graph.is_split_graph.qmd) |
| Walks | [`is_eulerian()`](../reference/Graph.is_eulerian.qmd), [`is_semieulerian()`](../reference/Graph.is_semieulerian.qmd), [`has_eulerian_path()`](../reference/Graph.has_eulerian_path.qmd), [`has_cycles()`](../reference/Graph.has_cycles.qmd), [`has_bridges()`](../reference/Graph.has_bridges.qmd) |

These are useful as guards, since many algorithms assume a property such as connectedness or
acyclicity, and as quick facts about a graph:

```{python}
karate.is_connected(), karate.is_bipartite(), karate.is_planar()
```

The karate club is connected, but it isn't bipartite (it has triangles) or planar (it can't be
drawn without crossing edges).

## Degrees

A node's degree is its number of edges, and in a directed graph each node has an in-degree and an
out-degree as well. [`degrees()`](../reference/Graph.degrees.qmd) computes every node's degree, and
follows the usual convention for algorithms: it stores the result in a `degree` attribute by
default, and returns it as a dictionary with `return_dict=True`.

The *degree distribution*, the number of nodes with each degree, is the most important single
description of a network's structure. [`degree_distribution()`](../reference/Graph.degree_distribution.qmd)
returns it as a dictionary from degree to count:

```{python}
sorted(karate.degree_distribution().items())
```

Eleven members have just two friends, while two have 16 and 17. Such a skewed distribution, with
many low-degree nodes and a few hubs, is typical of social networks, and it's quite unlike the
narrow, bell-shaped distribution of a random graph of the same density (see
[Graph generators](05-generators.qmd#the-classic-models)).

For a larger network, the node table and Polars give a fuller picture. In the power grid, nearly
nine nodes in ten have degree four or less, as befits a network of physical lines between
substations:

```{python}
import polars as pl

grid = ec.power_grid()
(
    grid.get_node_df()
    .group_by("degree")
    .len()
    .sort("degree")
    .with_columns(share=pl.col("len") / pl.col("len").sum())
    .head(6)
)
```

[`average_neighbor_degree()`](../reference/Graph.average_neighbor_degree.qmd) computes, for each
node, the mean degree of its neighbors. It reveals the "friendship paradox": in most networks,
your friends have more friends than you do, simply because popular people appear in many friend
lists. Member `"11"` (ID 12), for instance, has a single friend, who is the instructor:

```{python}
karate.get_degree(12), karate.average_neighbor_degree(return_dict=True)[12]
```

## Distances

The distance between two nodes is the number of edges on the shortest path between them (or the
total weight, for weighted measures; see [Paths and distances](12-paths.qmd)). A handful of
measures summarize the distances of a whole graph:

| Measure | Meaning | Method |
|---|---|---|
| Eccentricity | a node's distance to the node farthest from it | [`eccentricity()`](../reference/Graph.eccentricity.qmd) |
| Diameter | the largest eccentricity: the longest shortest path | [`diameter()`](../reference/Graph.diameter.qmd) |
| Radius | the smallest eccentricity | [`radius()`](../reference/Graph.radius.qmd) |
| Center | the nodes whose eccentricity equals the radius | [`center()`](../reference/Graph.center.qmd) |
| Periphery | the nodes whose eccentricity equals the diameter | [`periphery()`](../reference/Graph.periphery.qmd) |
| Barycenter | the nodes with the smallest total distance to all others | [`barycenter()`](../reference/Graph.barycenter.qmd) |
| Mean distance | the average over all pairs of nodes | [`mean_distance()`](../reference/Graph.mean_distance.qmd) |
| Global efficiency | the average of the inverse distances | [`global_efficiency()`](../reference/Graph.global_efficiency.qmd) |

```{python}
karate.radius(), karate.diameter(), round(karate.mean_distance(), 2)
```

No two members are more than five steps apart, and the typical pair is between two and three steps
apart: the karate club is a small world. Eight members have the smallest eccentricity, three, so
they form the center, but only the instructor minimizes the *total* distance to everyone else:

```{python}
karate.center(), karate.barycenter()
```

The center and the barycenter answer slightly different questions. The center minimizes the
worst case, so it's the right place for something that must reach everyone, such as a fire
station. The barycenter minimizes the average, so it suits something that everyone uses, such as a
shop.

The mean distance and the diameter are infinite in a disconnected graph. EdgeCase computes them
over the pairs that are connected, so they describe the typical distance within components.
[`global_efficiency()`](../reference/Graph.global_efficiency.qmd), the mean of the *inverse*
distances, handles disconnection more gracefully, since an unreachable pair simply contributes 0.

## Mixing patterns

Do nodes link to similar nodes? *Assortativity* answers this with a correlation coefficient
between −1 and 1, computed over the edges.

**By degree.** [`assortativity_degree()`](../reference/Graph.assortativity_degree.qmd)
measures whether high-degree nodes link to other high-degree nodes (positive values) or to
low-degree ones (negative values). Social networks of collaboration tend to be assortative, while
technological and biological networks tend to be disassortative, with hubs connected to many small
nodes. Comparing several of the bundled networks, simplified to remove the duplicate edges and
self-loops some of them contain (see [Datasets](06-datasets.qmd#networks-from-data-repositories)),
shows the pattern:

```{python}
networks = {
    "co-authorship (ca_grqc)": ec.ca_grqc().simplify(),
    "jazz musicians": ec.jazz().simplify(),
    "power grid": grid,
    "Internet": ec.internet().simplify(),
    "metabolism (celegans)": ec.celegans().simplify(),
    "karate club": karate,
}
{name: round(graph.assortativity_degree(), 3) for name, graph in networks.items()}
```

The physicists who wrote general relativity papers together are strongly assortative: prolific
authors write with other prolific authors, often in large collaborations. The jazz musicians and
the power grid are close to neutral. The Internet's hubs
connect to many small networks, which makes it disassortative, as is the metabolic network. The
karate club is the most disassortative of all, since its two hubs, the instructor and the
administrator, have many friends who have few friends of their own.

**By attribute.** [`assortativity_nominal()`](../reference/Graph.assortativity_nominal.qmd)
does the same for a categorical attribute, and
[`assortativity()`](../reference/Graph.assortativity.qmd) for a numeric one. The karate
club's two factions are strongly assortative, as expected of the groups the club split into:

```{python}
round(karate.assortativity_nominal("faction"), 3)
```

The *mixing matrix* behind the coefficient shows exactly where the edges fall.
[`attribute_mixing_matrix()`](../reference/Graph.attribute_mixing_matrix.qmd) returns the matrix
and the attribute values its rows and columns stand for, and `normalized=False` gives counts
rather than fractions:

```{python}
karate.attribute_mixing_matrix("faction", normalized=False)
```

Each edge is counted in both directions, so of the 78 friendships, 33 are within faction 1, 35
within faction 2, and only 10 cross between them. [`degree_mixing_matrix()`](../reference/Graph.degree_mixing_matrix.qmd)
is the degree equivalent.

### Reciprocity

In a directed graph, *reciprocity* measures how often a relationship is returned: the fraction of
edges `A -> B` for which `B -> A` also exists. In Wikipedia's administrator elections, votes are
rarely returned:

```{python}
round(ec.wiki_vote().reciprocity(), 3)
```

Only about 6% of votes are reciprocated, which fits a network in which established editors vote on
newcomers' candidacies. Friendship and communication networks usually have much higher
reciprocity. [`which_mutual()`](../reference/Graph.which_mutual.qmd) and
[`count_mutual_node_pairs()`](../reference/Graph.count_mutual_node_pairs.qmd) find the
reciprocated pairs themselves.

## Cores and dense regions

Many networks have a dense core surrounded by a sparser periphery. The *k-core* of a graph is the
largest subgraph in which every node has at least `k` neighbors, found by repeatedly removing the
nodes with fewer. A node's *coreness* is the largest `k` for which it belongs to the k-core.

| Method | Returns |
|---|---|
| [`coreness()`](../reference/Graph.coreness.qmd) | each node's coreness, stored as an attribute or returned as a dictionary |
| [`k_core()`](../reference/Graph.k_core.qmd) | the k-core, as a new graph |
| [`k_shell()`](../reference/Graph.k_shell.qmd), [`k_crust()`](../reference/Graph.k_crust.qmd), [`k_corona()`](../reference/Graph.k_corona.qmd) | the nodes of coreness exactly `k`, the nodes outside the k-core, and the k-core nodes with exactly `k` neighbors in it |
| [`k_truss()`](../reference/Graph.k_truss.qmd) | the largest subgraph in which every edge lies in at least `k - 2` triangles |
| [`densest_subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.densest_subgraph.qmd) | the set of nodes with the most edges per node |

```{python}
core = karate.k_core(4)
core.count_nodes(), core.count_edges()
```

The 4-core holds ten members and 25 of the club's friendships. Coloring the club by coreness shows
how the core sits among the rest:

```{python}
karate.coreness().plot(color_by="coreness", size_by="degree", label_by="label", seed=7)
```

The *k-truss* is a stricter version of the same idea. Requiring each edge to lie in triangles,
rather than each node to have neighbors, makes it a good detector of tightly knit groups:

```{python}
truss = karate.k_truss(4)
truss.count_nodes(), truss.count_edges()
```

[`densest_subgraph()`](../reference/Graph.densest_subgraph.qmd) takes a different approach, finding
the set of nodes with the highest ratio of edges to nodes, without any threshold to choose. It
returns the ratio and the nodes:

```{python}
density, members = karate.densest_subgraph()
density, len(members)
```

The densest part of the club has 16 members with 2.625 edges per member, which is to say an average
degree of 5.25 within the group.

### Cliques

A *clique* is a set of nodes that are all linked to one another, the densest structure possible.
[`find_cliques()`](../reference/Graph.find_cliques.qmd) lists every *maximal* clique (one that
can't be extended by another node), [`maximum_clique()`](../reference/Graph.maximum_clique.qmd)
finds a largest one, and [`clique_number()`](../reference/Graph.clique_number.qmd) gives its size:

```{python}
len(karate.find_cliques()), karate.maximum_clique()
```

The karate club has 36 maximal cliques, and the largest has five members: the instructor and four
of their closest friends. Finding the largest clique is a hard problem in general, but it is fast
on sparse real networks. [`node_clique_number()`](../reference/Graph.node_clique_number.qmd) gives
the size of the largest clique containing each node, and
[`enumerate_all_cliques()`](../reference/Graph.enumerate_all_cliques.qmd) lists every clique,
maximal or not.

### Rich clubs

The *rich-club coefficient* asks whether the high-degree nodes are more densely connected to one
another than chance would predict. [`rich_club_coefficient()`](../reference/Graph.rich_club_coefficient.qmd)
returns, for each degree `k`, the density of the subgraph of nodes with degree greater than `k`.
With `normalized=True`, it divides by the same quantity in degree-preserving randomizations of the
graph, so values above 1 indicate a rich club.

## Small worlds

A small-world network combines short paths, like a random graph, with high clustering, unlike one.
Two indices compare a graph against random and lattice references to quantify this.
[`small_world_sigma()`](../reference/Graph.small_world_sigma.qmd) is greater than 1 for a small
world, and [`small_world_omega()`](../reference/Graph.small_world_omega.qmd) runs from −1 (lattice
like) through 0 (small world) to 1 (random like). Both build many randomized graphs, so they are
slow on large networks; `iterations=` and `nrand=` trade accuracy for speed:

```{python}
round(karate.small_world_sigma(iterations=20, nrand=5, seed=1), 2)
```

[Clustering and motifs](15-clustering-and-motifs.qmd) has more on clustering coefficients, and
[Graph generators](05-generators.qmd#null-models-from-an-existing-graph) on the random references
these comparisons are made against.
